maps/mile-markers:
How mile markers are numbered

The small green signs along a highway are called reference location signs in the federal sign manual, the MUTCD. The 2023 edition requires them on all freeways, in part so crashes and emergencies can be located. They also help drivers judge progress and help with highway maintenance.

Zero is at the south or west state line, or where the route begins inside the state. On a divided highway the distance is measured on the northbound or eastbound side. The sign for the other direction goes directly across from it, so both sides show the same number at the same spot. Signs go on the right side of the road, or in the median where the right side won't work, up to 30 feet from the pavement.

Interstate mile numbers generally start over at each state line. Northbound on I-75, Florida's markers pass 470 near the Georgia line, and Georgia's begin again near zero. Some states also run county-based systems, covered in the list below.

Tenths and enhanced markers

States may add intermediate markers every tenth, two tenths or half mile. When they do, the whole-mile marker shows a decimal and a zero, such as 42.0. Some states use enhanced markers instead. Those are vertical green signs with the direction on top, then the route shield, then the mile. The intermediate version adds the tenth on a bottom line. Both are optional, so you will see them in some states and not others.

Exit numbers use the same count

The MUTCD requires exit numbers to match the posted mile markers and says consecutive numbering shall not be used. Its guidance is that a crossroad meeting the highway between mile 15 and mile 16 becomes exit 15. When interchanges sit too close to number by the mile, letters split them. The manual's example is 256A. Once 256A exists, there can't also be a plain exit 256 in the same direction.

The manual says this numbering helps drivers report their location after a crash or breakdown and helps responders reach them. It also means a new interchange doesn't force a renumbering. On a beltway that circles a city, exits are numbered clockwise, starting near the south end of the loop.

Some states switched around 2000. Georgia renumbered its interstate exits in 1999 and 2000, and exit 18 on I-75 at Tifton became exit 62. Florida moved I-4 and most of its other interstates to mile-based exits in 2002. Directions written before the change use the old numbers.

Where the numbers work differently

  • California. Caltrans posts postmiles, and they restart at zero at each county line. A postmile only means something with its county attached. A letter in front, such as R, marks a realigned stretch with its own numbering. Exit numbers are separate. Caltrans numbers each exit by its distance from the start of the route, so I-5's last exit before Oregon is 796. More in California mile markers.
  • Texas. The small green placards with three-digit numbers on state highways are TxDOT reference markers. TxDOT places them every 2 miles on state-maintained roads and every mile on interstates. More in Texas mile markers.
  • Nevada. NDOT posts two kinds. Green interstate markers count from the state line. White and black standard mileposts count from the county line, and US and state routes use county mileage only. A two-letter county code sits under the route, such as CL for Clark. Where an interstate shares the road with another route, only the interstate appears on the post. More in Nevada mile markers.
  • Shared highways. Where two routes run on the same pavement, the count continues for only one of them, and an interstate keeps its numbers. Past the overlap, the MUTCD says the other route's first marker should show the total distance traveled on that route, so it lines up with your odometer again.

Why a pin may not match the sign

The pins on this map come from DOT milepost records, and positions are approximate. The MUTCD lets a sign move as much as 50 feet from its measured spot when it can't go in the right place. If it can't be placed within 50 feet, the MUTCD recommends leaving it out.

Roads also change. A realigned curve or a rebuilt interchange can move a sign while the record stays put. If the map and the roadside marker differ, report the number on the sign along with the highway, direction and state.

Using markers on a trip

On one route inside one state, subtracting markers gives distance. From mile 120 to mile 175 is 55 miles. Across a state line the count resets, so add what is left in the first state to the marker you reach in the next. The math stops working where the route shares pavement with another highway or follows a county-based system.

To find your own number, use What mile marker am I at? For the two numbering systems side by side, read mile markers vs exit numbers. For how interstates get their route numbers, see how interstates are numbered.
what-mile-marker-am-i-at:
Finding the number without a phone

Mile markers are usually small green signs with white numbers. Nevada's dispatch guide notes that some around Las Vegas are white with black numbers. Look on the right shoulder first. Where there is no room on the right, some are in the median. They can sit up to 30 feet from the pavement, so scan past the guardrail.

The count starts at the south or west state line, or where the route begins, and climbs as you head north or east. The sign for the other direction sits directly across the road and shows the same number. On major highways they come every mile. At 60 mph that is one a minute, so if you missed one, watch for the next.

Two markers in a row also tell you your direction. If the numbers are going up, you are heading north or east on that route. If they are going down, you are heading south or west.

Some states add markers every tenth, two tenths or half mile, so you may read 42.3 or 42.5. Others post enhanced markers with the direction on top and the route shield under it. One of those tells you the highway, the direction and the mile in a single glance.

Use the exit number

Exit numbers come from the same count. Federal sign rules say a crossroad that meets the highway between mile 15 and mile 16 should be exit 15. If you can't see a marker, give dispatch the last exit you passed, your direction, and about how far you have gone since. A letter after the number, as in 15A and 15B, means more than one exit shares that mile number. They can be ramps at one interchange or separate interchanges close together. The letters run in alphabetical order in the direction the numbers climb, so heading the other way you reach 15B before 15A. On a beltway, the MUTCD says exits are numbered clockwise, starting near the south end of the loop.

Directions written before a state switched to mile-based numbering use the old exit numbers. Georgia switched in 1999 and 2000. Florida switched most of its interstates in 2002. The signs on the road are current.

What to tell dispatch

The mile marker is the first thing dispatch asks for on a highway. Nevada's highway patrol dispatch guide asks callers for these.

  • The highway. The route number, such as I-15 or US-95.
  • The marker or exit. The one you are near or just passed.
  • The direction. The way you are heading, or the way the vehicle or hazard is going.

The guide's own example is "I-15 northbound passing milemarker 17." For debris or a stalled car, it asks which lane, counting the far-left lane as lane one. It also notes that 911 will transfer you to the right agency. If you are driving, pull over before you call, or hand the phone to a passenger.

In Florida, *FHP (*347) reaches the Florida Highway Patrol to report a crash or a stranded driver. For more on the call itself, read what to tell 911 after a highway breakdown.

If no marker is in sight

On a two-lane road, the MUTCD lets a state post markers on one side only, sometimes back to back on one post. Your number may be on the far side of the road.

In a city, use the cross street or exit name. Nevada's dispatch guide gives "US-95 southbound passing Rainbow" as a good report. A rest area or the last town you passed also helps. Say which way you are heading and whether the landmark is behind you or ahead.

Why the lookup can be off

GPS.gov says GPS-enabled phones are typically accurate to about 16 feet under open sky. Buildings and tree cover make it worse. On a computer without GPS, the browser falls back on whatever the device offers, such as Wi-Fi location, which is less exact.

This page shows the nearest recorded milepost, not a point between two posts. Near an interchange, the closest post can belong to the road crossing over you. If the route shown doesn't match the shield on the road, trust the sign. What highway am I on? can help confirm it.

Where the numbers reset

Interstate mile numbers generally restart at state lines, and some reference systems restart at county lines. Mile 5 in Kentucky and mile 5 in Ohio are about 190 miles apart on I-75, so name the state when you are near a border.

A few places count differently. California posts postmiles that restart at each county line, so a postmile needs its county. In Nevada, green interstate markers count from the state line, while white and black mileposts count from the county line and carry a county code such as CL for Clark. Where two highways share a road, the count continues for only one of them, and an interstate keeps its numbers over a US or state route. On Texas state highways, the small green three-digit placards are TxDOT reference markers, posted every 2 miles, or every mile on interstates.

The mile marker map shows recorded posts in every state. Mile markers vs exit numbers explains the two systems side by side.
corridors/i-75:
Mile markers restart at every state line

Each state numbers its own section of I-75 from its southern line, and exit numbers follow the same count. These are the lengths of each state's section, so they are also about where each state's numbers end.

  • Florida. About 471 miles.
  • Georgia. About 355 miles.
  • Tennessee. About 162 miles.
  • Kentucky. About 192 miles.
  • Ohio. About 211 miles.
  • Michigan. About 396 miles, to Sault Ste. Marie.

Name the state when you give a location near a border. Mile 5 in Kentucky and mile 5 in Ohio are about 190 miles apart.

Stretches to check before you go

Alligator Alley, Florida

Between Naples and the Fort Lauderdale area, I-75 is a 78-mile toll road across the Everglades. There is a toll plaza at each end and two untolled interchanges in between. Rates change, so check Florida's Turnpike before the trip. In a rental, read whether to take the rental car's toll pass.

Metro Atlanta express lanes

Georgia runs reversible express lanes on I-75 on both sides of Atlanta. The Northwest Corridor lanes cover 29.7 miles on I-75 and I-575. They typically run southbound in the morning and northbound in the evening, so check the posted direction before you enter. The South Metro lanes run 12 miles through Henry and Clayton counties. Both need an accepted toll transponder. Peach Pass works, and so do E-ZPass, SunPass, E-Pass and NC Quick Pass accounts. Tractor-trailers and vehicles towing trailers can't use them. Prices rise with demand. See I-75 in Georgia.

Fog at the Hiwassee River, Tennessee

Tennessee runs a fog detection and warning system on I-75 at the Hiwassee River crossing near Calhoun. Sensors watch about three miles of road, and the warning zone starts eight miles out on each approach. When the system detects fog, it can post reduced speed limits on message signs and close the ramps with gates. Treat a lowered limit there as a fog warning for the road ahead.

The Brent Spence Bridge, Cincinnati

I-71 and I-75 share the Brent Spence Bridge over the Ohio River between Covington and Cincinnati. Construction of a companion bridge began in 2026, with opening planned for about 2031. Ramp closures and relocations on the approaches come with it. Check the Cincinnati cameras before you cross.

The Mackinac Bridge, Michigan

I-75 crosses the Straits of Mackinac on a toll bridge. The Mackinac Bridge Authority sets restrictions by sustained wind, not gusts.

  • 20 to 35 mph. High wind advisory. High-profile vehicles go no faster than 20 mph.
  • 35 to 50 mph. High-profile vehicles wait for an escort.
  • 50 to 65 mph. High-profile vehicles are barred. Cars towing nothing may cross at 20 mph or less.
  • 65 mph or higher. The bridge closes to all traffic.

High-profile includes pickups with campers, anything towing a boat, and cars with bikes or cargo on the roof. The authority can restrict traffic at lower speeds when other hazards are present. See I-75 in Michigan.
corridors/i-15:
How high I-15 climbs

I-15's highest point is Monida Pass, 6,870 feet, on the Idaho and Montana line. Here is how the other summits compare.

  • Mountain Pass, California. 4,730 feet, near the Nevada line.
  • Beaver County, Utah. 6,611 feet at about mile 125, near the Sulphurdale interchange. This is the high point in Utah.
  • Monida Pass. 6,870 feet on the Continental Divide.

Between Barstow and the state line, Halloran Summit also tops 4,000 feet. I-15 crosses into Nevada at Primm, about 40 miles southwest of Las Vegas. Southbound, California's agricultural inspection station is at Mountain Pass, about 4 miles past the Nevada line. CDFA opened it in 2018 to replace the old station at Yermo.

Check Utah, Idaho and Montana road conditions before a winter drive north of Salt Lake City.

The Virgin River Gorge

I-15 spends 29.4 miles in Arizona, all of it in Mohave County and isolated from the rest of Arizona's highways. The gorge begins around mile 13. Limestone cliffs rise as high as 500 feet above the road, and five bridges cross the Virgin River inside the canyon. Arizona's exits run from 8 at Beaver Dam and Littlefield to 27 at Black Rock Road.

Express lanes in San Diego and Utah

In San Diego, SANDAG's I-15 Express Lanes run 20 miles in the median from SR-163 to SR-78 in Escondido. Solo drivers need FasTrak. The San Diego cameras page has more.

In Utah, express lanes run on I-15 between Riverdale and Spanish Fork. Carpools of two or more, motorcycles and buses use them without a toll. Vehicles pulling trailers and vehicles over 18,000 pounds gross weight are not allowed. Solo drivers need an Express Pass set to toll mode, and tolls run from 25 cents to $2 per zone. UDOT lists a fine of $337 or more for driving alone without one. Enter and leave only where the lines are dashed. Crossing the double white lines is illegal.

Mile markers by state

I-15's numbers restart at each state line. Utah's section is 400.6 miles long, so its markers run from 0 at the Arizona line to about 400 at Idaho. California works differently. Exit numbers there count miles from the start of the route, while Caltrans postmiles restart at each county line. On the California section, give the nearest exit, or a postmile with its county.
corridors/i-4:
Mile markers and exit numbers on I-4

I-4 starts at the I-275 interchange in Tampa, known locally as Malfunction Junction. That is mile 0. The numbers climb east to the I-95 interchange near Daytona Beach at about mile 132.

Florida switched I-4 from sequential exit numbers to mile-based ones in 2002. Directions written before then use the old numbers. The Beachline Expressway, SR 528, is now exit 72. It used to be exit 28. SR 417 is now exit 62, once 24C through 24E.

I-4 Express through Orlando

The I-4 Ultimate project added four express toll lanes along 21 miles, from Kirkman Road (SR 435, exit 75) to SR 434 (exit 94). They opened on February 26, 2022. Tolls go up and down with traffic. There is no cash and no toll-by-plate. You need a SunPass or another transponder Florida accepts, such as E-ZPass, E-PASS or Peach Pass. Trucks with three or more axles and vehicles pulling trailers or boats are not allowed. See rental car toll passes if you are in a rental.

FDOT plans to extend the express lanes about 40 more miles to the southwest and northeast. Those segments are in planning and design. The Daryl Carter Parkway interchange, exit 70, opened in July 2025.

Fog, smoke and rain

Fog and smoke have caused major crashes on I-4 near Polk City, where morning fog has mixed with smoke from planned burns. Check visibility reports and the cameras before an early drive through Polk County.

Since July 1, 2023, Florida law allows hazard lights while driving in periods of extremely low visibility, on roads posted 55 mph or higher. The law does not define a visibility distance. A Florida trooper told WKMG that flashers signal something is wrong, which can confuse the drivers around you. Check the road weather map before you leave or while parked.

Help on the road

FDOT's Road Rangers patrol I-4 and give limited roadside help at no charge, such as changing a tire. To request one, or to report a crash or a stranded driver, dial *FHP (*347). Pull over first. FL511 posts lane closures and live cameras for I-4. Florida's move over law covers Road Ranger trucks too. Since January 1, 2024, it also covers any disabled vehicle stopped with hazard lights, flares or emergency signs. If you can't change lanes, slow to 20 mph below the posted limit.
passes/cajon:
The grade, exit by exit

California exit numbers count miles from the start of the route, so they work as a rough mile marker on the climb. The postmiles on roadside markers restart at each county line.

  • Exit 123. The I-215 junction at Devore. Southbound traffic can exit here toward San Bernardino, and northbound I-215 traffic joins I-15.
  • Exit 124. Kenwood Avenue.
  • Exit 129. Cleghorn Road.
  • Exit 131. SR-138, toward Palmdale and Silverwood Lake.
  • Exit 138. Oak Hill Road, past the summit.
  • Exit 143. Main Street in Hesperia.

The northbound and southbound lanes separate on the climb and rejoin shortly before Cajon Summit. Southbound, the descent toward Devore has a runaway truck ramp.

Wind and fire

The National Weather Service names the Cajon Pass corridor as one of three main Santa Ana wind corridors around the Los Angeles Basin. NWS forecasts for strong events have called for gusts of 70 mph or more below the pass. If you are towing or driving something tall, read the forecast before you go.

Wildfires have closed both directions of I-15 through Cajon Pass. In fire season, check closures and fire information before you leave. The wildfire map and the cameras above are a start.

If I-15 is closed

SR-138 heads west from exit 131 toward Palmdale and is mostly a two-lane road. East of I-15, it passes Silverwood Lake, then turns narrow and twisting before it ends at SR-18 south of Crestline. When Caltrans or CHP posts a detour, take that one.

Before you leave, check Caltrans QuickMap or call 1-800-427-7623 for chain controls and closures. In San Bernardino and Riverside counties, dialing 511 reaches IE511. California's chain rules are on California chain laws.
cameras:
How to read a DOT camera image

Start with the time stamp. Most of these are still frames, and each agency refreshes them on its own schedule. Caltrans District 2, in the far north of the state, says its still images could update more often than once an hour, but the extra communication would cost more. If a time stamp is old, the camera may have lost power or its connection. District 2 says some remote sites are hard to reach in deep snow and stay down longer.

A camera aimed straight at the ground may be getting cleaned. District 2 has a preset that points the lens down so operators can clear snow and rain from it.

Don't count on the images being saved. UDOT, for one, says its camera footage generally is not recorded. If you need proof for an insurance claim, start with what to record after a crash.
cameras/atlanta:
The Downtown Connector

Through central Atlanta, I-75 and I-85 share one freeway for about 7.5 miles. It is 12 to 14 lanes wide. Heading north at the split, I-75 takes the right three lanes toward the northwest and I-85 takes the left three toward the northeast. Pick your lane well before the split.

Trucks and the Perimeter

Georgia law bars commercial vehicles, buses included, from driving through the I-285 Perimeter on I-75, I-85, I-20 and GA 400 without business inside it. Pickups, deliveries, terminals, repair shops and a driver's own home count. Through trucks use I-285. Fines run from $150 to $1,000 per violation, plus court costs.

Express lanes

Metro Atlanta's express lanes need an accepted toll transponder. A Peach Pass works, and so do E-ZPass, SunPass, E-Pass and NC Quick Pass accounts. Prices rise with demand, with a minimum of 10 cents a mile. Vehicles with more than two axles or six wheels can't use them, except over-the-road buses. Trailers and tractor-trailers are not allowed. A Peach Pass also works on Florida's I-4 Express lanes in Orlando.

  • I-75 and I-575 Northwest Corridor. 29.7 miles, reversible. Typically southbound in the morning and northbound in the evening. Follow the posted direction.
  • I-75 South Metro. 12 reversible miles from SR 155 in Henry County to SR 138 in Clayton County.
  • I-85 in Gwinnett. 15 miles from Chamblee Tucker Road to Old Peachtree Road, then 10 more to Hamilton Mill Road.

When you need help

GDOT's HERO crews patrol about 400 miles of metro Atlanta interstates around the clock. They clear crashes and debris and help with flat tires and dead batteries at no charge. Request help through 511 or 511GA. When you pass a HERO truck working a scene, slow down and move over a lane. See Georgia's move over law.

After a minor crash with no serious injuries, Georgia law (O.C.G.A. 40-6-275) requires moving a car that still drives out of the travel lanes, to the shoulder, emergency lane or median, if it can be done safely. Moving it does not make you at fault. You still have to report the crash as the law requires. Georgia law also bars holding a phone while driving, so look at these cameras before you leave or let a passenger check them. Check each image's time stamp, since conditions on the Connector change within minutes. See how long crashes take to clear.
cameras/utah:
Before you drive the Cottonwood canyons

Big Cottonwood Canyon (SR-190) and Little Cottonwood Canyon (SR-210) fall under UDOT's Class 3 traction requirements, the strictest class in the traction law. When the beacons outside the canyons flash, every vehicle needs at least 5/32 inch of tread. All-wheel and four-wheel drive vehicles need at least M+S tires on all wheels. Two-wheel drive vehicles need three-peak mountain snowflake tires on all wheels, or chains or other traction devices on at least two drive wheels. UDOT can put the rules in place 24 hours before a storm. A windshield sticker from UDOT's inspection program shows the car passed. See Little Cottonwood and Utah chain laws.

Mile markers on I-15 in Utah

Utah's section of I-15 is 400.6 miles long. Markers start at 0 at the Arizona line near St. George and reach about 400 at the Idaho line. Exit numbers use the same count. The highest point is 6,611 feet at about mile 125 in Beaver County, near the Sulphurdale interchange.

I-15 express lanes

From Riverdale to Spanish Fork, I-15 has express lanes. Vehicles with two or more people ride without a toll. A solo driver needs a UDOT Express Pass in toll mode. Vehicles towing trailers are not allowed. Get in and out only where the lane lines are dashed. Details are on the I-15 corridor page.

UDOT's own sources

UDOT Traffic, on the web and as an app, puts the cameras next to road weather and restrictions. You can also dial 511. UDOT says its camera footage generally is not recorded or saved. Check each image's time stamp before you judge conditions, and look again right before you leave.
cameras/san-diego:
Reading a postmile label

Caltrans locates points with postmiles, not statewide mile markers. A postmile starts at zero at the county line or the start of the route and climbs as you head north or east. It restarts at the next county line. That is why every label on this map carries the county.

A letter in front of the number changes it. R marks a realigned section, measured on its own. When you report a location by postmile, include the full label, prefix and all, and the county.

Exit numbers count from the start of the route

Exit numbers work differently. Caltrans numbers each exit by its distance from the beginning of the route. On I-5, exit 1 is just north of the Mexican border, and the count runs to 796 before Oregon. When you tell someone where you are, give the nearest exit if you know it. If you have a Caltrans postmile, include the county and any prefix.

I-15 Express Lanes

SANDAG runs 20 miles of express lanes in the I-15 median between SR-163 and SR-78 in Escondido. Movable barriers shift lanes toward the busier direction. Carpools and motorcycles pay no toll. Solo drivers need a FasTrak transponder, and the toll changes with traffic.

I-8 east into the mountains

East of the city, I-8 climbs above 4,000 feet at Laguna Summit, 4,055 feet. Exit 47 there leads to Sunrise Highway and Mount Laguna, where the county sets chain controls in winter storms. Storms can also bring snow to I-8 itself, and the National Weather Service has issued high wind advisories for I-8 from Alpine to the Imperial County line. Check Caltrans QuickMap or call 1-800-427-7623 before you go.

Other sources

Caltrans District 11 runs the state highways in San Diego and Imperial counties. Its QuickMap app and website show lane closures, chain controls and CHP incidents on the state highway system. Dial 511 anywhere in San Diego County for SANDAG's 511 service, call 1-855-GO-SD-511 from outside the county, or use 511sd.com. I-5 begins at the border at the San Ysidro Port of Entry. Commercial trucks can't cross there and use Otay Mesa, reached by SR-905. Headed to Mexico? See border wait times.
cameras/georgia:
Exit numbers changed around 2000

Georgia renumbered its interstate exits in 1999 and 2000. The old system counted exits one after another. The new one counts miles from the state line or from where the interstate begins. Exit 30 on I-16 near Savannah became exit 148, and exit 18 on I-75 in Tifton became exit 62. Directions and paper maps from before the change use the old numbers.

Roadside help outside Atlanta

Outside metro Atlanta, GDOT's CHAMP crews patrol the interstates, except I-59 and I-24. They help with flat tires and dead batteries, and they report road damage and debris to GDOT. Dial 511 for help or to report a problem. CHAMP is a separate program from HERO. Inside metro Atlanta, GDOT's HERO crews handle interstate incident response and roadside help. GDOT asks drivers to slow down and move over a lane when CHAMP is working. See Georgia's move over law.

I-16 contraflow for hurricanes

When the coast is under a mandatory evacuation, GDOT can reverse the eastbound lanes of I-16. All lanes then carry westbound traffic from Savannah to US 441 in Dublin, about 125 miles. The crossover into the reversed lanes is at the I-95 interchange near Savannah. If you get on I-16 west of I-95, you stay in the normal westbound lanes. A second crossover west of Dublin returns traffic to the normal side.

Phone rules while driving

Since July 1, 2018, Georgia drivers may not hold or support a phone with any part of their body while driving. That includes stops at red lights. Calls through a speaker, earpiece or car system are allowed, and so is GPS navigation. Set up the cameras or your route before you leave, or let a passenger check them. A first conviction carries a fine of up to $50 and one point on your license. A first charge for holding a phone can end in not guilty if you show the court a device that lets you talk without holding the phone, or proof you bought one.

Before any storm drive, check Georgia road conditions and the road weather map.
cameras/ohio:
Ohio Turnpike tolls and exit numbers

The Ohio Turnpike runs 241 miles across northern Ohio. It carries I-80 from Indiana to North Jackson, I-90 from Indiana to Elyria, and I-76 for the last 22.6 miles to Pennsylvania. The Ohio Turnpike and Infrastructure Commission runs it, not ODOT. Since April 2024, E-ZPass drivers pay at highway speed. Drivers paying with cash or a card stop at a gate when they exit. Exit numbers follow the turnpike's own mileage.

Lake-effect snow on I-90

East of Cleveland, lake-effect snow off Lake Erie can make nearby sections of I-90 look very different from each other. NWS Cleveland's lake-effect warnings often cover Lake, Geauga and Ashtabula counties. I-90 runs through that belt, and storms have closed it in Ashtabula County up to the Pennsylvania line. Before you leave, check camera time stamps, road restrictions and NWS warnings along your route. See I-90 conditions.

The Brent Spence Bridge

I-71 and I-75 cross the Ohio River together on the Brent Spence Bridge between Cincinnati and Covington. Work on a companion bridge began in 2026. ODOT expects it to open in 2031, with approach work through 2033. Expect closed and relocated ramps near the bridge, including from US 50. See Cincinnati cameras.

OHGO

ODOT's OHGO site and app show cameras, travel times and construction. The app can send alerts for a commute you save.

Phone rules while driving

Since April 2023, Ohio law bars using, holding or supporting a phone while driving, and police can stop you for that alone. You may use the speakerphone if you don't hold the phone. Navigation directions are allowed as long as you don't hold or support the device. A first offense carries a fine of up to $150 and two points. Under the version in effect since June 30, 2025, an eligible first-time offender can take an approved distracted driving course instead of paying the fine and getting the points. Check cameras before you leave or hand the phone to a passenger.
closures:
Closed, closed to through traffic, or one lane

A full closure blocks ordinary traffic past the closure point, though authorized vehicles may still go through. A lane closure leaves at least one lane open, and this map leaves those out. The signs tell you which you are facing. Under the MUTCD, a ROAD CLOSED sign goes where a road is closed to all traffic except authorized vehicles. ROAD CLOSED TO THRU TRAFFIC and ROAD CLOSED, LOCAL TRAFFIC ONLY mean the road stays open to local traffic up to the closure point. BRIDGE OUT can replace ROAD CLOSED when a bridge is the problem. An advance sign can warn of the closure ahead, with a distance or a cross street on it, so you can turn off before the barricade.

Why a closure can outlast the crash

FHWA tracks two clocks for a crash. Roadway clearance ends when all lanes are open again. Incident clearance ends when the last responder leaves. A road can reopen while crews are still on the shoulder.

A 2010 FHWA publication cited research estimating that the chance of a secondary crash rises 2.8% for each minute the first crash stays a hazard. When you reach a scene, slow down and move over. For typical times, see how long crashes take to clear. For the path from a crash scene to a state feed, read how a crash report reaches your phone.
bridges:
Who runs each bridge

The Seattle Department of Transportation owns the Ballard, Fremont and University bridges and the Spokane Street swing bridge. WSDOT runs the Montlake Bridge on SR 513 and the First Avenue South Bridge on SR 99. King County runs the South Park Bridge, which opened in 2014 to replace a span from 1931.

When the bridges can stay down

Federal law gives boats the right of way over cars, but Coast Guard rules set commute windows. The Ballard, Fremont and University bridges need not open from 7 to 9 a.m. or 4 to 6 p.m., Monday through Friday, for vessels under 1,000 gross tons. The limit does not apply to a vessel towing one of 1,000 gross tons or more, and it does not apply on federal holidays other than Columbus Day. A bridge may also hold a boat for up to 10 minutes to clear built-up traffic, though boats towing get no wait. From 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., boats must call the Fremont drawtender an hour ahead.

Montlake has longer windows. From September 1 to April 30 it need not open 7 to 10 a.m. or 3:30 to 7 p.m. on weekdays. The rest of the year, the windows are 7 to 9 a.m. and 3:30 to 6:30 p.m. From 12:30 to 3:30 p.m. and from 6 to 6:30 p.m., it opens for those vessels only on the hour and half hour. On the Duwamish, the First Avenue South Bridge need not open on weekdays from 6 to 9 a.m. and 3 to 6 p.m. That limit does not apply to vessels of 5,000 gross tons or more, or to a vessel towing one or heading to tow one. The South Park Bridge need not open on weekdays from 6:30 to 8:30 a.m. and 3:30 to 5:30 p.m. From 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. it opens with 12 hours' notice, and within 45 minutes when emergency responders need it. Details are on Seattle drawbridge opening rules.

How long you wait

SDOT says a Ballard or Fremont opening averages about four minutes from stopping traffic to letting it go. WSDOT lists average openings of 4 minutes for Montlake and 11 minutes for First Avenue South. Add time for the line of cars to move once the gates go up.

Fremont has about 30 feet of vertical clearance, so taller boats need an opening. SDOT counted an average of about 35 openings a day. Montlake has 46 feet of clearance and First Avenue South has 48.

More about the bridges

Fremont opened in 1917. Ballard Bridge, also from 1917, is 2,854 feet long and connects Ballard with Magnolia and Queen Anne.

In February 2026, inspectors found cracks in the steel deck grates of the northbound First Avenue South Bridge. Crews replaced nine failing panels with 10 new steel grid deck panels over two weekend closures in May 2026. Design is under way to replace the remaining panels, with construction expected to start in 2027. The bridge stayed open to boats through the repairs. Check closures before you rely on SR 99 northbound.

The BNSF railroad bridge at the canal's west end opens on signal at any hour.

The Aurora Bridge on SR 99 and the I-5 Ship Canal Bridge cross high above the canal and do not open. See how long Seattle bridge openings last and the Fremont Bridge page.
